title: Analytic Distribution of Classifier-Free Guidance for Schedule Design

paper.title: Analytic Distribution of Classifier-Free Guidance for Schedule Design
paper.abstract: Abstract Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is the default mechanism for conditional generation in diffusion models, but the distribution sampled by its deterministic guided dynamics is not captured by the usual product-distribution heuristic p 0 ω ​ q 0 1 − ω p_{0}^{\omega}q_{0}^{1-\omega} . We analyze CFG through the probability flow ODE and derive exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distributions for both constant and time-dependent guidance. The resulting formulas show that CFG modifies p t 0 p_{t_{0}} by an exponential path-integral correction, and that a time-dependent schedule enters this correction through the weight ω ⁡ ( t ) − 1 \omega(t)-1 . This characterization explains how score discrepancies accumulate along sampling trajectories and motivates Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG), a schedule that balances timestep contributions while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score-error amplification. A toy model with analytic scores closely verifies the predicted distributions. On Stable Diffusion 1.5, DG-CFG improves generation and yields a stronger diversity–fidelity trade-off across guidance strengths, with especially clear gains when strong guidance causes saturation and quality degradation in constant and heuristic schedules. Across NFE budgets, DG-CFG reaches fixed image-quality targets with fewer sampling steps, reducing the sampling cost needed to achieve target metrics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] have emerged as a leading paradigm in generative modeling, achieving state-of-the-art results across image synthesis [ 4 , 5 ] , video generation [ 6 ] , audio synthesis [ 7 ] , and molecular conformation generation [ 8 ] . Their operating principle is conceptually elegant: a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE) progressively corrupts data with noise, and a learned reverse process—parameterized by the score function—removes this noise to reconstruct realistic samples. This framework, unified by Song et al. [ 3 ] , admits two equivalent reverse-time descriptions: a stochastic SDE and a deterministic probability flow ODE that preserves the same marginal distributions at every timestep. For conditional generation, classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 9 ] has become the de facto standard. Unlike classifier-based guidance [ 4 ] , which requires an auxiliary classifier, CFG blends the score functions of a conditional model p data p_{\mathrm{data}} and a reference model q data q_{\mathrm{data}} (typically the unconditional model) through a guidance strength parameter ω \omega : s t ω ​ ( x ) = ω ​ ∇ x ​ log ⁡ p t ​ ( x ) + ( 1 − ω ) ​ ∇ x ​ log ⁡ q t ​ ( x ) . s_{t}^{\omega}(x)=\omega\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}(x)+(1-\omega)\nabla_{x}\log q_{t}(x). (1) When ω > 1 \omega>1 , the conditional score is extrapolated beyond the reference score, often improving visual quality and prompt alignment but reducing sample diversity and causing supersaturation. Because it requires neither auxiliary networks nor additional training, this simple extrapolation underpins modern text-to-image systems [ 5 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] and has also been adopted in video [ 6 ] , audio [ 13 ] , and 3D synthesis [ 14 ] . Despite this empirical success, a basic distributional question remains unresolved: what distribution does CFG actually sample from? A common intuition is that CFG samples from the normalized product distribution r ~ 0 ∝ p 0 ω ​ q 0 1 − ω \tilde{r}_{0}\propto p_{0}^{\omega}q_{0}^{1-\omega} , since s t ω s_{t}^{\omega} is the score of p t ω ​ q t 1 − ω p_{t}^{\omega}q_{t}^{1-\omega} at each fixed time t t . This pointwise interpretation, however, does not by itself characterize the distribution produced by the full reverse-time dynamics. The blended score is applied throughout the sampling trajectory, and the accumulated effect of these time-dependent perturbations is not captured by the terminal product distribution alone. Resolving this question is practically important: an exact characterization can clarify how CFG departs from the naïve product picture, explain failure modes such as mode collapse and color oversaturation, and guide the design of principled time-dependent schedules. Existing theoretical studies have provided explanations of failure modes, product-distribution heuristics, stagewise dynamics, correction mechanisms and so on, but they do not directly characterize the sampling distribution induced by the deterministic CFG reverse process. In this work, we characterize the distribution produced by CFG within the deterministic probability flow ODE framework. By deriving and solving the Fokker–Planck equations associated with the guided reverse process, we obtain exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distribution under both constant and time-dependent guidance. These formulas reveal a simple organizing principle: guidance modifies the target distribution through an exponential path-integral correction whose effective temporal weight is governed by ω ⁡ ( t ) − 1 \omega(t)-1 . We then use this principle to design a guidance schedule and validate both the theory and the schedule experimentally. Our main contributions are: 1. Theory: exact analytic distribution of CFG. We derive exact analytic path-integral representations of the CFG-induced distribution under constant guidance (Theorem 4.3 ) and time-dependent guidance (Theorem 4.4 ). Both representations have the same structural form: r ^ t 0 ​ ( x ) \hat{r}_{t_{0}}(x) equals p t 0 ​ ( x ) p_{t_{0}}(x) multiplied by an exponential path-integral correction. In the time-dependent case, the correction is weighted by ω ⁡ ( t ) − 1 \omega(t)-1 , with constant CFG recovered as the degenerate case ω ⁡ ( t ) ≡ ω \omega(t)\equiv\omega . The analysis also identifies an interaction potential between the conditional and reference scores, clarifying how score discrepancies accumulate along sampling trajectories and contribute to CFG’s mode-concentrating behavior. 2. Schedule: a principled guidance schedule. The path-integral formulation shows that, under the standard VPSDE noise schedule, the diffusion coefficient β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) varies by roughly two orders of magnitude. As a result, constant CFG implicitly overweights the high-noise regime. Guided by the fact that ω ⁡ ( t ) − 1 \omega(t)-1 controls the per-timestep contribution to the path integral, we construct Distribution-Guided Classifier-Free Guidance (DG-CFG): ω ⁡ ( t ) = 1 + C ⋅ ( ω ¯ − 1 ) ⋅ ( 1 − α ¯ t ) ​ α ¯ t β ⁡ ( t ) , \omega(t)=1+C\cdot(\bar{\omega}-1)\cdot\frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{\beta(t)}, where the three factors respectively compensate for β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) non-uniformity, temporal variation in signal content, and score-approximation error amplification in the low-noise regime. 3. Experiments: verification and validation. On a toy model with analytic score functions, empirical DDIM samples closely match the distributions predicted by Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 under both constant and time-dependent guidance. On Stable Diffusion 1.5, DG-CFG is evaluated against constant and heuristic baselines across guidance strengths, ablations, and sampling-step budgets, demonstrating improved robustness at high guidance strengths, better saturation control, and consistently strong image-quality metrics. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 fixes notation and reviews diffusion models, classifier-free guidance, and the Fokker–Planck equation. Section 3 discusses related work on diffusion models, CFG variants, theoretical analyses of CFG, and guidance schedule design. Section 4 develops the main theory: it formulates the CFG sampling problem, derives the Fokker–Planck equation for the normalized product reference distribution, and obtains exact analytic path-integral representations of the deterministic CFG-induced distribution under constant and time-dependent guidance. Section 5 specializes the theory to the VPSDE/DDIM setting and derives DG-CFG by correcting the temporal imbalance induced by the noise schedule, signal content, and low-noise score-error amplification. Section 6 first verifies the theoretical distributions on a toy model with analytic scores, then evaluates DG-CFG on Stable Diffusion 1.5 through comparisons across guidance strengths, component-wise ablations, NFE sweeps, and fixed-quality sampling-step analyses. Section 7 summarizes the paper and discusses future directions. All proofs and toy model analytic formulas are collected in the appendix.

sections.heading: 3.1 Diffusion Models
sections.text: Diffusion models generate samples by learning to reverse a Markovian noising process. The foundational framework was introduced by Sohl-Dickstein et al. [ 1 ] and popularized by Ho et al. [ 2 ] with DDPM. Song et al. [ 3 ] unified diffusion models and score-based generative modeling through SDEs, connecting denoising diffusion with score matching [ 18 , 19 ] . Deterministic samplers such as DDIM [ 16 ] are closely related to the probability flow ODE, which preserves the same time marginals while enabling faster sampling. Subsequent advances have improved sample quality [ 4 , 20 ] , accelerated inference [ 21 , 22 ] , and extended diffusion models to latent spaces [ 5 , 23 ] . Our analysis builds on the probability flow ODE viewpoint and asks how CFG changes the distribution transported by these deterministic dynamics.

sections.heading: 3.2 Classifier-Free Guidance and Variants
sections.text: Classifier-free guidance was proposed by Ho and Salimans [ 9 ] as an alternative to classifier-based guidance [ 4 ] . By jointly training conditional and unconditional score models, CFG removes the need for a separately trained classifier while retaining strong conditional generation performance. It has become a standard component of large-scale text-to-image systems [ 5 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] and has been extended to video [ 6 ] , audio [ 13 ] , and 3D synthesis [ 14 ] . Several variants have been proposed to address known failure modes. CFG++ [ 24 ] applies guidance only to the denoised estimate while using the unconditional prediction for re-noising, which reduces off-manifold errors and improves invertibility. Dynamic thresholding [ 10 ] adaptively clips and rescales the CFG-predicted clean image at each sampling step, mitigating color oversaturation at high guidance scales. Karras et al. [ 25 ] apply autoguidance using a smaller or less-trained version of the model itself as the reference model. Adaptive projected guidance (APG) [ 26 ] decomposes the CFG update into components parallel and orthogonal to the conditional prediction, identifies the parallel component as a major source of oversaturation, and rescales it to suppress artifacts at high guidance strengths. These methods improve practical behavior, but they do not directly characterize the probability distribution induced by score blending along the reverse trajectory.

sections.heading: 3.3 Theoretical Understanding of CFG
sections.text: Despite CFG’s practical ubiquity, its theoretical understanding remains limited. Bradley and Nakkiran [ 27 ] showed that CFG should not be interpreted as directly sampling a gamma-powered product distribution under either DDPM or DDIM; instead, in the SDE limit, it can be viewed as a predictor-corrector procedure combining conditional denoising with a Langevin-style sharpening step. Pavasovic et al. [ 28 ] studied CFG in high-dimensional settings, showing that it recovers the target conditional distribution in the infinite-dimensional limit, while finite-dimensional corrections produce mean overshoot and variance shrinkage. Jin et al. [ 29 ] developed a theory for CFG under multimodal conditional distributions, showing that guided sampling can proceed through direction shift, mode separation, and concentration stages, thereby motivating time-varying guidance schedules. Skreta et al. [ 30 ] introduced Feynman–Kac correctors for sampling from product distributions with pretrained diffusion models, using sequential Monte Carlo to correct the CFG heuristic. Gao et al. [ 31 ] analyzed score discrepancies between conditional and unconditional distributions across timesteps, deriving bounds that motivate a time-dependent control function for guidance strength. Our contribution is complementary to these works. Rather than focusing on a particular failure mode, justifying a product-distribution approximation, or adding external correction terms, we derive an exact analytic path-integral representation of the density r ^ t 0 \hat{r}_{t_{0}} induced by the deterministic guided reverse process. The resulting characteristic formulas characterize the distribution induced by CFG under the probability flow ODE, up to normalization.

sections.heading: 3.4 Guidance Schedule Design
sections.text: Varying guidance strength over the sampling trajectory is not new. Several works have observed that the optimal guidance strength may differ between the coarse high-noise phase and the fine low-noise phase of generation. Simple schedules such as linear ramps or step functions have also been explored heuristically [ 10 ] . More recently, time-varying schedules have been proposed: β \beta –CFG [ 32 ] uses a beta-distribution-shaped curve to suppress guidance near both endpoints of the trajectory, while interval guidance [ 33 ] applies CFG only within a selected noise-level window, showing that guidance can be harmful at very high noise levels and unnecessary at very low noise levels. These results support the importance of temporal allocation, but the functional forms are not derived from the induced distributional representation itself. In Section 5 , we derive a schedule from the path-integral structure of our distributional representation.

sections.heading: 4 Distribution of Classifier-Free Guidance
sections.text: We now analyze the distribution produced by CFG under the deterministic probability flow ODE ( 8 ), without committing to a specific parameterization of f ⁡ ( x , t ) f(x,t) and g ⁡ ( t ) g(t) . We first formulate the sampling problem (Section 4.1 ), then derive the Fokker–Planck equation for the normalized product reference distribution (Section 4.2 ). We next obtain an exact analytic path-integral representation under constant guidance (Section 4.3 ) and extend the result to time-dependent guidance schedules (Section 4.4 ).

sections.heading: 5.1 Motivation: Why Constant Guidance is Suboptimal
sections.text: With constant guidance ω ⁡ ( s ) ≡ ω ¯ \omega(s)\equiv\bar{\omega} , the schedule-dependent weight reduces to β ​ ( s ) ​ ( ω ¯ − 1 ) \beta(s)(\bar{\omega}-1) . In the standard VPSDE with a linear continuous noise rate β ⁡ ( s ) = β min + s ⁡ ( β max − β min ) / T \beta(s)=\beta_{\min}+s(\beta_{\max}-\beta_{\min})/T (typical values: β min = 0.1 \beta_{\min}=0.1 and β max = 20 \beta_{\max}=20 ), the high-noise end ( s ≈ T s\approx T ) receives a coefficient roughly 200 200 times larger than the low-noise end ( s ≈ t 0 s\approx t_{0} ). Thus, a nominally constant guidance strength does not produce a constant contribution to the path integral; the effective per-timestep guidance weight is modulated by two orders of magnitude. This imbalance has visible consequences. The high-noise phase primarily determines coarse semantic layout, global structure, and color, whereas the low-noise phase refines details and textures. When constant CFG is combined with a rapidly increasing β ⁡ ( s ) \beta(s) , guidance is concentrated disproportionately in the high-noise regime. This can encourage repeated coarse layouts and color bias, reducing global diversity and increasing oversaturation. Meanwhile, the low-noise regime receives comparatively little effective guidance, which can leave fine details under-refined. These effects become more pronounced at large guidance strengths because the entire path-integral correction is amplified by ω ¯ − 1 \bar{\omega}-1 .

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate our theory and the resulting schedule in two stages. First, we use a controlled toy model in which all relevant scores and path-integral terms admit analytic closed forms, enabling direct verification of Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 (Section 6.1 ). sections.heading: 6.2 Stable Diffusion 1.5
sections.text: We next evaluate the proposed schedule on Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) [ 5 ] . Unlike the toy model, SD1.5 uses neural score approximators on 64 × 64 64\times 64 latent representations, bringing the analysis into a practical large-scale generation setting. We first compare guidance strategies across a range of nominal guidance strengths ω ¯ \bar{\omega} at a fixed sampling budget. We then isolate the contribution of each DG-CFG component through ablations (Section 6.2.3 ) and study robustness to the number of function evaluations (NFE) in the high-guidance regime.

sections.heading: 6.2.1 Setup
sections.text: We use the official SD1.5 checkpoint from RunwayML. 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5 The unconditional score is obtained with an empty text prompt, and the conditional score uses prompts from the MS-COCO 2017 validation set [ 34 ] . All images are generated with the DDIM sampler [ 16 ] . For each method, we randomly select N = 1,000 N=1{,}000 prompt–image pairs from MS-COCO 2017 and generate one 512 × 512 512\times 512 image per prompt. We evaluate overall image quality with Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [ 35 ] , prompt alignment with CLIP score [ 36 ] , and perceptual quality with ImageReward (IR). We also report a saturation diagnostic (Sat) to detect the color over-saturation pathology that commonly appears under strong guidance. CLIP, IR, and Sat are averaged over the N N generated images, while Vendi score is averaged over the N div N_{\mathrm{div}} prompts. For reference, real MS-COCO images achieve CLIP = 30.57 \text{CLIP}=30.57 , IR = 0.38 \text{IR}=0.38 , and Sat = 0.33 \text{Sat}=0.33 under the same evaluators.

sections.heading: 6.2.2 Main Results
sections.text: We compare four guidance strategies at ω ¯ ∈ { 3 , 7 , 11 , 15 , 19 , 23 } \bar{\omega}\in\{3,7,11,15,19,23\} using the same DDIM sampler with 8 8 NFE: • Constant CFG: ω ⁡ ( t ) ≡ ω ¯ \omega(t)\equiv\bar{\omega} . • Interval CFG [ 33 ] : ω ⁡ ( t ) = 1 + ( ω ¯ − 1 ) / 0.6 \omega(t)=1+(\bar{\omega}-1)/0.6 for t ∈ [ 200,800 ] t\in[200,800] , ω ⁡ ( t ) = 1 \omega(t)=1 otherwise. • β \beta –CFG [ 32 ] : ω ⁡ ( t ) = ω ¯ ⋅ 6 ⋅ ( t / T ) ⋅ ( 1 − t / T ) \omega(t)=\bar{\omega}\cdot 6\cdot(t/T)\cdot(1-t/T) . • DG-CFG (ours): ω ⁡ ( t ) = 1 + C ⋅ ( ω ¯ − 1 ) ⋅ ( 1 − α ¯ t ) ​ α ¯ t / β ⁡ ( t ) \omega(t)=1+C\cdot(\bar{\omega}-1)\cdot(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}/\beta(t) , with C = 1 / 0.0270 C=1/0.0270 . All non-constant schedules are normalized so that ∫ t 0 T ( ω ⁡ ( s ) − 1 ) ​ 𝑑 s = ( ω ¯ − 1 ) ​ T \int_{t_{0}}^{T}(\omega(s)-1)\,ds=(\bar{\omega}-1)T . Thus, differences across methods reflect how guidance is distributed over time rather than differences in the total guidance budget. Table 2 reports the quantitative results, and Figure 2 provides representative samples. We summarize the main observations below. Diversity–fidelity trade-off. At low-to-moderate guidance strengths, DG-CFG improves diversity over constant CFG while maintaining comparable FID. For example, at ω ¯ = 7 \bar{\omega}=7 , DG-CFG increases the Vendi score from 5.40 5.40 to 5.71 5.71 with essentially unchanged FID ( 67.67 67.67 vs. 67.87 67.87 ). This is consistent with the path-integral interpretation: by preventing the high-noise regime from dominating the correction, the sampler retains more variation in coarse semantic layout. At very large guidance strengths, diversity scores must be interpreted jointly with fidelity and saturation. Constant CFG shows an apparent increase in Vendi score at ω ¯ = 19 \bar{\omega}=19 and 23 23 , but this coincides with rapidly worsening FID, negative IR, and strong color over-saturation. These samples occupy an unnatural region of feature space, so the diversity increase is not a desirable improvement. Image-quality improvement at high guidance. At moderate guidance ( ω ¯ ≤ 7 \bar{\omega}\leq 7 ), DG-CFG has slightly lower IR than the strongest baseline, reflecting a small cost for increased diversity. The trend reverses as guidance grows: DG-CFG is the only method whose IR becomes positive and remains positive from ω ¯ = 15 \bar{\omega}=15 onward, while the baselines degrade. DG-CFG also maintains competitive CLIP scores and the best FID among all methods at ω ¯ ∈ { 15 , 19 , 23 } \bar{\omega}\in\{15,19,23\} , indicating that the schedule remains stable in the high-guidance regime where constant and heuristic schedules deteriorate. In this regime, DG-CFG achieves the strongest overall image-quality profile among the evaluated methods, reaching state-of-the-art performance within this comparison on IR, FID, and high-guidance CLIP. Saturation control. The Sat metric diagnoses the common color over-saturation pathology under strong guidance. As ω ¯ \bar{\omega} increases, constant CFG, Interval CFG, and β \beta –CFG all exceed the real-image reference level ( 0.33 0.33 ) by a wide margin. DG-CFG stays below this level up to ω ¯ = 19 \bar{\omega}=19 and reaches it only at the most extreme setting, ω ¯ = 23 \bar{\omega}=23 . Its saturation values also change more gradually across guidance strengths, indicating substantially more stable color behavior than the baselines. Qualitative visualization. Figure 2 shows representative samples across methods and guidance strengths for two prompts. As ω ¯ \bar{\omega} increases, the baselines exhibit progressively stronger color over-saturation and structural degradation: images become posterized, fine textures are washed out, and object boundaries lose definition. DG-CFG maintains more natural color balance and coherent structure across the full guidance range, including ω ¯ = 23 \bar{\omega}=23 . sections.heading: 6.2.3 Ablation Study
sections.text: To isolate the contribution of each design component, we compare four progressively more complete schedules at ω ¯ ∈ { 3 , 7 , 11 , 15 , 19 , 23 } \bar{\omega}\in\{3,7,11,15,19,23\} using 8 8 NFE. Each variant has its own normalization constant, chosen so that the integrated guidance deviation matches that of constant CFG. • Constant CFG: ω ⁡ ( t ) ≡ ω ¯ \omega(t)\equiv\bar{\omega} (baseline). • Medium 1: ω ⁡ ( t ) = 1 + C 1 ⋅ ( ω ¯ − 1 ) / β ⁡ ( t ) \omega(t)=1+C_{1}\cdot(\bar{\omega}-1)/\beta(t) (time-balance only). • Medium 2: ω ⁡ ( t ) = 1 + C 2 ⋅ ( ω ¯ − 1 ) ⋅ α ¯ t / β ⁡ ( t ) \omega(t)=1+C_{2}\cdot(\bar{\omega}-1)\cdot\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}/\beta(t) ( + +\, signal-content weighting). • DG-CFG (ours): ω ⁡ ( t ) = 1 + C 3 ⋅ ( ω ¯ − 1 ) ⋅ ( 1 − α ¯ t ) ​ α ¯ t / β ⁡ ( t ) \omega(t)=1+C_{3}\cdot(\bar{\omega}-1)\cdot(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}/\beta(t) (all three factors). Table 3 reports the quantitative results. We analyze the components in the same order as the schedule construction in Section 5 , focusing on how each factor changes diversity, fidelity, perceptual quality, and saturation as guidance becomes stronger. Step 1: time-balance (Medium 1 vs. constant). Normalizing by β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) consistently improves diversity and substantially reduces saturation, with the effect becoming more pronounced as ω ¯ \bar{\omega} increases. At extreme guidance, constant CFG suffers from severe over-saturation and deteriorating perceptual quality, whereas time balancing alone keeps saturation much closer to the real-image reference and improves FID. This supports the diagnosis in Section 5 : preventing the high-noise regime from dominating the path integral is the main mechanism for controlling saturation-driven degradation. The trade-off is weaker performance at low guidance, where Medium 1 has lower CLIP, IR, and FID than constant CFG. Step 2: Signal-content weighting (Medium 2 vs. Medium 1). Adding α ¯ t \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}} further increases diversity and produces the lowest saturation values among all variants. This confirms that signal-content weighting shifts guidance toward timesteps where clean signal is present. However, the shift comes at a substantial cost: CLIP, IR, and FID degrade across the full guidance range, and the degradation persists at high ω ¯ \bar{\omega} . This is consistent with the analysis in Section 5 : emphasizing low-noise timesteps exposes the sampler to score-approximation errors amplified by 1 / σ t 2 1/\sigma_{t}^{2} , leading to unnatural textures and reduced realism. Signal-content weighting is therefore useful but incomplete on its own. Step 3: Score-error mitigation (DG-CFG vs. Medium 2). Adding the ( 1 − α ¯ t ) (1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}) factor mitigates this low-noise score-error amplification. DG-CFG restores image quality relative to Medium 2 while retaining much of the diversity and saturation control gained by the first two steps. At moderate-to-high guidance, it is the only variant whose IR becomes positive and remains positive; at ω ¯ = 23 \bar{\omega}=23 , it also achieves substantially better FID than constant CFG and Medium 2 while keeping saturation close to the real-image reference. The ablation therefore shows that time balancing, signal-content weighting, and score-error mitigation play complementary roles. The qualitative samples in Figure 3 show the same pattern. Constant CFG exhibits visible color over-saturation and limited fine detail. Medium 1 improves color behavior and produces more varied samples, but its images remain less faithful. Medium 2 further increases variation and detail but introduces unnatural textures and structural artifacts. DG-CFG resolves this trade-off most effectively: it preserves the diversity and detail introduced by the intermediate schedules while recovering more realistic textures, natural color, and coherent structure. sections.heading: 6.2.5 Minimal NFE to Reach Fixed Quality Targets
sections.text: The NFE sweep above compares methods at equal sampling budgets. We now ask the converse question: given a fixed quality target, how many sampling steps does each method require to reach it? This fixed-quality view is practically relevant because it measures the inference cost needed to attain a prescribed output quality. We fix ω ¯ = 23 \bar{\omega}=23 , a high-guidance regime that is both challenging and informative. Strong guidance accentuates common artifacts such as color over-saturation and amplifies discretization errors, making the effect of NFE easier to observe. At the same time, if these artifacts are controlled, this regime offers the greatest potential for improving prompt alignment and perceptual quality. We consider five targets: three ImageReward thresholds ( IR ≥ 0 \text{IR}\geq 0 , IR ≥ 0.1 \text{IR}\geq 0.1 , and IR ≥ 0.2 \text{IR}\geq 0.2 ), one text-alignment threshold ( CLIP ≥ 30.5 \text{CLIP}\geq 30.5 ), and one distributional-quality threshold ( FID ≤ 75 \text{FID}\leq 75 ). In practical terms, the proposed schedule can lower latency and computational cost without sacrificing the target level of image quality.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied classifier-free guidance through the deterministic probability flow ODE and derived exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distribution. The resulting characterization shows that CFG modifies the target distribution through an exponential path-integral correction, whose temporal contribution is governed by ω ⁡ ( t ) − 1 \omega(t)-1 . This perspective explains how guidance accumulates along the sampling trajectory and motivates DG-CFG, a schedule that balances the path-integral contribution across timesteps while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score errors. Experiments on a controlled toy model closely match the theoretical predictions. Large-scale evaluation on Stable Diffusion 1.5 further shows that DG-CFG improves the diversity–fidelity trade-off across guidance strengths and NFE budgets, with stronger saturation control than constant and heuristic baselines. Fixed-quality comparisons indicate that DG-CFG achieves comparable image quality with fewer sampling steps, and component-wise ablations confirm that each factor in the schedule contributes to its performance. Limitations and Future Work. The proposed schedule corrects temporal non-uniformities in the noise schedule, but it does not explicitly optimize the geometric structure of the score discrepancy. Extending the theoretical analysis to flow matching models is a natural direction and may lead to analogous guidance principles for a broader class of generative models. August 24, 2026 1 Introduction Diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] have emerged as a leading paradigm in generative modeling, achieving state-of-the-art results across image synthesis [ 4 , 5 ] , video generation [ 6 ] , audio synthesis [ 7 ] , and molecular conformation generation [ 8 ] . Their operating principle is conceptually elegant: a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE) progressively corrupts data with noise, and a learned reverse process—parameterized by the score function—removes this noise to reconstruct realistic samples. [ 3 ] , admits two equivalent reverse-time descriptions: a stochastic SDE and a deterministic probability flow ODE that preserves the same marginal distributions at every timestep. For conditional generation, classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 9 ] has become the de facto standard. Because it requires neither auxiliary networks nor additional training, this simple extrapolation underpins modern text-to-image systems [ 5 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] and has also been adopted in video [ 6 ] , audio [ 13 ] , and 3D synthesis [ 14 ] . The blended score is applied throughout the sampling trajectory, and the accumulated effect of these time-dependent perturbations is not captured by the terminal product distribution alone. Resolving this question is practically important: an exact characterization can clarify how CFG departs from the naïve product picture, explain failure modes such as mode collapse and color oversaturation, and guide the design of principled time-dependent schedules. We use it to compare the evolution of the normalized product reference distribution with the true density transported by the guided probability flow ODE, which leads to the exact analytic path-integral characterizations in Section 4 . 3 Related Work 3.1 Diffusion Models Diffusion models generate samples by learning to reverse a Markovian noising process. The foundational framework was introduced by Sohl-Dickstein et al. [ 1 ] and popularized by Ho et al. [ 2 ] with DDPM. Song et al. [ 3 ] unified diffusion models and score-based generative modeling through SDEs, connecting denoising diffusion with score matching [ 18 , 19 ] . Deterministic samplers such as DDIM [ 16 ] are closely related to the probability flow ODE, which preserves the same time marginals while enabling faster sampling. Subsequent advances have improved sample quality [ 4 , 20 ] , accelerated inference [ 21 , 22 ] , and extended diffusion models to latent spaces [ 5 , 23 ] . Our analysis builds on the probability flow ODE viewpoint and asks how CFG changes the distribution transported by these deterministic dynamics. 3.2 Classifier-Free Guidance and Variants Classifier-free guidance was proposed by Ho and Salimans [ 9 ] as an alternative to classifier-based guidance [ 4 ] . By jointly training conditional and unconditional score models, CFG removes the need for a separately trained classifier while retaining strong conditional generation performance. It has become a standard component of large-scale text-to-image systems [ 5 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] and has been extended to video [ 6 ] , audio [ 13 ] , and 3D synthesis [ 14 ] . Several variants have been proposed to address known failure modes. CFG++ [ 24 ] applies guidance only to the denoised estimate while using the unconditional prediction for re-noising, which reduces off-manifold errors and improves invertibility. Dynamic thresholding [ 10 ] adaptively clips and rescales the CFG-predicted clean image at each sampling step, mitigating color oversaturation at high guidance scales. Karras et al. [ 25 ] apply autoguidance using a smaller or less-trained version of the model itself as the reference model. Adaptive projected guidance (APG) [ 26 ] decomposes the CFG update into components parallel and orthogonal to the conditional prediction, identifies the parallel component as a major source of oversaturation, and rescales it to suppress artifacts at high guidance strengths. These methods improve practical behavior, but they do not directly characterize the probability distribution induced by score blending along the reverse trajectory. 3.3 Theoretical Understanding of CFG Despite CFG’s practical ubiquity, its theoretical understanding remains limited. Bradley and Nakkiran [ 27 ] showed that CFG should not be interpreted as directly sampling a gamma-powered product distribution under either DDPM or DDIM; instead, in the SDE limit, it can be viewed as a predictor-corrector procedure combining conditional denoising with a Langevin-style sharpening step. Pavasovic et al. [ 28 ] studied CFG in high-dimensional settings, showing that it recovers the target conditional distribution in the infinite-dimensional limit, while finite-dimensional corrections produce mean overshoot and variance shrinkage. Jin et al. [ 29 ] developed a theory for CFG under multimodal conditional distributions, showing that guided sampling can proceed through direction shift, mode separation, and concentration stages, thereby motivating time-varying guidance schedules. Skreta et al. [ 30 ] introduced Feynman–Kac correctors for sampling from product distributions with pretrained diffusion models, using sequential Monte Carlo to correct the CFG heuristic. Gao et al. [ 31 ] analyzed score discrepancies between conditional and unconditional distributions across timesteps, deriving bounds that motivate a time-dependent control function for guidance strength. Our contribution is complementary to these works. Rather than focusing on a particular failure mode, justifying a product-distribution approximation, or adding external correction terms, we derive an exact analytic path-integral representation of the density r ^ t 0 \hat{r}_{t_{0}} induced by the deterministic guided reverse process. The resulting characteristic formulas characterize the distribution induced by CFG under the probability flow ODE, up to normalization. 3.4 Guidance Schedule Design Varying guidance strength over the sampling trajectory is not new. Several works have observed that the optimal guidance strength may differ between the coarse high-noise phase and the fine low-noise phase of generation. Simple schedules such as linear ramps or step functions have also been explored heuristically [ 10 ] . More recently, time-varying schedules have been proposed: β  eta –CFG [ 32 ] uses a beta-distribution-shaped curve to suppress guidance near both endpoints of the trajectory, while interval guidance [ 33 ] applies CFG only within a selected noise-level window, showing that guidance can be harmful at very high noise levels and unnecessary at very low noise levels. These results support the importance of temporal allocation, but the functional forms are not derived from the induced distributional representation itself.
